First, we express $f(x)=5\operatorname{ln}⁡(3-2x)+7$ as the composite function

$$
f=5\operatorname{ln}⁡u+7,\,u=3-2x.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}=\frac{5}{u},\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-2.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =\frac{5}{u}\cdot (-2) \\  & =-\frac{10}{u} \\  & =-\frac{10}{3-2x}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
Let $g(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(4-3x)$ and $h(x)=3x.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =g(x)+h(x).\end{aligned}
$$

First, we differentiate $g(x).$ We express $g(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(4-3x)$ as the composite function

$$
g=\operatorname{ln}⁡u,\,u=4-3x.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}g}{\text{d}u}=\frac{1}{u},\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-3.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}g}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}g}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =\frac{1}{u}\cdot (-3) \\  & =-\frac{3}{u} \\  & =-\frac{3}{4-3x}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate $h(x)=3x:$ 

$$
\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}x}=3
$$

Hence,

$$
{f}^{′}(x)={g}^{′}(x)+{h}^{′}(x)=-\frac{3}{4-3x}+3.
$$

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we express $f(x)$ as the composite function

$$
f = \ln u, \qquad u = x^2-4.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d f}{\textrm d u} = \dfrac{1}{u},\qquad \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm d x} = 2x.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =\frac{1}{u}\cdot 2x \\  & =\frac{1}{{x}^{2}-4}\cdot 2x \\  & =\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}-4}.\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
The chain rule can be used to differentiate logarithmic functions like 

$$
y = \ln (2x+1).
$$

First notice that this function can be written as the composite function

$$
y = \ln u, \qquad u = 2x+1.
$$

We can use the chain rule to compute the derivative of this composite function:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}(\operatorname{ln}⁡u)\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2x+1) \\  & =\frac{1}{u}\cdot 2 \\  & =\frac{2}{u}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $u=2x+1,$ we obtain the final result:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{2}{2x+1}\end{aligned}
$$
